passage: Microorganisms, or germs, are invisible to the naked eye and exist everywhere, even on surfaces that appear perfectly clean. Because they are microscopic, you cannot rely on your eyes to judge if your hands are safe; they may harbor pathogens even when they look spotless. Effective handwashing is the most critical defense against these invisible threats. Simply rinsing with water is insufficient because germs are often protected by natural oils on our skin that water alone cannot remove. Using plain soap for at least twenty seconds is essential, as soap molecules physically break down the oily layer and lift germs away, regardless of whether the soap is labeled antibacterial. Furthermore, germs do not only spread through direct contact with sick individuals; they travel through contaminated surfaces and respiratory droplets. When you cough or sneeze, you must cover your mouth with a tissue or your elbow rather than your bare palm, as palms easily transfer pathogens to everything you touch. Finally, remember that antibiotics are specialized medicines designed only to fight bacterial infections. They are completely ineffective against viruses like the common cold or flu. Taking them unnecessarily or stopping a prescribed course early contributes to antibiotic resistance, making future infections harder to treat. Always complete the full course of medicine as directed by your doctor to ensure the infection is fully eliminated.

items.evidence: Because they are microscopic, you cannot rely on your eyes to judge if your hands are safe; they may harbor pathogens even when they look spotless.
items.q: Meena's hands look spotless after playing outside. What can she conclude about germs on them?
options: They may be there but too small to see
There are none, since her hands look clean
They are there only if hands smell bad
They are there only if she met someone sick
items.explain: Germs are microscopic, so hands can carry them even when they look spotless.

wrong.why: thinks clean-looking hands have no germs
thinks germs come only from dirty or smelly things
thinks germs spread only from sick people

items.evidence: Simply rinsing with water is insufficient because germs are often protected by natural oils on our skin that water alone cannot remove.
items.q: Why is rinsing your hands with water alone not enough?
options: Because skin oils shield germs from the water
Because water is too cold to kill germs
Because germs hide only under visible dirt
Because water must be boiled before washing
items.explain: Natural skin oils protect germs, and water alone cannot remove those oils.

wrong.why: links germs and illness to cold water
thinks germs are only where dirt is visible
thinks water must be heated to work

items.evidence: Using plain soap for at least twenty seconds is essential, as soap molecules physically break down the oily layer and lift germs away, regardless of whether the soap is labeled antibacterial.
items.q: Asha has only an ordinary soap bar, not antibacterial soap. How should she wash?
options: Scrub all over with it for twenty seconds
Rinse with water, as plain soap won't work
Rub it for five seconds to kill germs
Scrub only her palms with it quickly
items.explain: Plain soap breaks the oily layer and lifts germs away when used for twenty seconds.

wrong.why: thinks a five-second rub is enough
thinks washing palms alone is enough

items.evidence: Furthermore, germs do not only spread through direct contact with sick individuals; they travel through contaminated surfaces and respiratory droplets.
items.q: Ravi never touched his sick classmate, yet caught the same illness. Which explains this?
options: He picked up germs from surfaces or droplets
He got wet in the rain that day
He must have touched the classmate unknowingly
He sat near something dirty and smelly
items.explain: Germs also travel through contaminated surfaces and droplets, not only by touching sick people.

wrong.why: thinks germs spread only by touching sick people
thinks germs come only from dirty things

items.evidence: When you cough or sneeze, you must cover your mouth with a tissue or your elbow rather than your bare palm, as palms easily transfer pathogens to everything you touch.
items.q: Tina feels a sneeze coming during class. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Sneeze into a tissue or her elbow
Sneeze into her palm, then wipe it
Cover her mouth only if she feels ill
Sneeze freely, since only touch spreads germs
items.explain: Palms pass germs to everything touched, so sneeze into a tissue or elbow.

wrong.why: thinks wiping the palm later is fine
thinks covering up is only for sick people
thinks germs spread only by direct touch
